title: The Physiological Cost of Flowering in Sugarcane: Why Genetic Correlations May Conceal Substantial Yield Penalties
content: Flowering in sugarcane is essential for genetic improvement but can reduce cane and sugar yield in commercial production. Experimental studies, including Australian work, have demonstrated flowering-associated yield losses, yet weak genetic correlations between flowering propensity, cane yield and commercial cane sugar have been interpreted as grounds for assigning little negative selection weight to flowering. We argue that these findings address different questions: genetic correlations describe associations among genotypes, whereas the physiological penalty is the yield foregone when a genotype flowers rather than remaining vegetative. A weak genetic correlation therefore cannot exclude a substantial causal penalty. We propose a developmental sink-strength hypothesis in which reproductive commitment both terminates the production of new vegetative phytomers and establishes reproductive carbon demand that may constrain biomass accumulation in internodes still developing at floral initiation. Reduced internode dimensions or functional storage tissue could subsequently limit sucrose mass even where sucrose concentration is maintained or temporarily increased. The contribution of this proposed mechanism to observed yield losses remains unquantified. We identify controlled within-genotype comparisons, internode-resolved measurements and field assessments across flowering and harvest conditions as priorities for separating physiological mechanisms and estimating commercial losses. Sugarcane selection should account for losses in harvestable cane biomass and recoverable sugar without compromising access to reproductively competent parents.
